This first cluster covers the paper's Physiology section (Q1-Q40, keyed on p8): 20 of its 37 usable items (Q1-Q12, Q14-Q20, Q22) are authored here; Q13, Q21 and Q39 are held (2-3 printed options, below the 4-option floor); Q23-Q38 and Q40 remain for a follow-up cluster. Four items (Q3, Q5, Q6, Q19) reuse an existing AU-MED-201 physiology concept minted from the Mock exam EGU 2023-2024 batch — same underlying fact, tested here from a different stem — rather than minting a near-duplicate.

questions.title: Normal arterial pH
questions.question: What is the normal arterial PH?

explanations.A: Correct. Arterial blood pH is tightly regulated by the bicarbonate buffer system, respiratory CO2 excretion and renal acid handling to a mean of about 7.40, with a normal range of roughly 7.36-7.44. This value is the reference point against which any acidosis or alkalosis is defined.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 7.38 ± 0.02 sits within the low-normal edge of the physiological range but is not the conventional reference mean taught for normal arterial pH.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 7.36 ± 0.02 is at the lower boundary of the normal range and would already be flagged as borderline acidemia on a blood gas, not the typical reference value.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 7.34 ± 0.02 falls below the normal range altogether and represents mild acidemia, not the normal arterial pH.

questions.learning_objective: State that normal arterial pH is approximately 7.40 ± 0.02.

questions.title: Normal glomerular filtration rate
questions.question: What is the normal GFR?

explanations.A: Correct. The average adult glomerular filtration rate is approximately 125 mL/min (roughly 180 L/day), a figure derived from inulin- or creatinine-based clearance studies. This value is the textbook reference for normal renal function and the denominator against which clinical estimated-GFR readings are compared. It reflects the combined filtering capacity of both kidneys' roughly two million nephrons in a healthy young adult.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 100 mL/min understates the standard teaching value; it is closer to a commonly quoted rounded clearance figure for other substances, not the reference GFR itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 110 mL/min is below the conventional 125 mL/min reference value for normal adult GFR.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 80 mL/min is well below normal GFR and would instead suggest at least moderate renal impairment, not a healthy adult's filtration rate.

questions.learning_objective: State that normal adult GFR is approximately 125 mL/min.

questions.title: Genuine anterior pituitary hormone
questions.question: Which of the following hormones is released from anterior pituitary?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Corticotrophin-releasing hormone (CRH) is a hypothalamic releasing hormone that acts on the anterior pituitary to stimulate ACTH release; it is not itself synthesised there.
explanations.B: Correct. Growth hormone is synthesised and secreted by somatotroph cells of the anterior pituitary itself, under hypothalamic GHRH/somatostatin control. Unlike the three distractors here, which are all hypothalamic releasing hormones that act upstream on the anterior pituitary, GH is a genuine anterior pituitary hormone. This distinction between hormones made by the anterior pituitary and hormones that merely regulate it is a recurring exam point for this gland.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) is a hypothalamic releasing hormone that stimulates anterior pituitary TSH release; it is not an anterior pituitary hormone itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) is a hypothalamic releasing hormone that stimulates anterior pituitary FSH/LH release; it is not synthesised by the anterior pituitary.

questions.learning_objective: Identify growth hormone as a genuine anterior pituitary hormone, distinguishing it from the hypothalamic releasing hormones CRH, TRH and GnRH.

field_notes.conceptReuse: Reuses CON-END-47B1788A21BEF9 (minted for the Mock exam's 'FSH is a genuine anterior pituitary hormone' item) — same discrimination (anterior pituitary hormone vs. hypothalamic releasing hormone), tested here with GH as the correct instance instead of FSH.

questions.title: Effect of sudden loss of the parathyroid glands
questions.question: What will happen to an adult if he suddenly loses his parathyroid glands?

explanations.A: Correct. Sudden loss of all parathyroid tissue removes parathyroid hormone's tonic support of plasma calcium, and plasma calcium falls acutely. Acute hypocalcemia increases neuromuscular excitability, producing tetany — skeletal muscle spasm, classically starting as carpopedal spasm (Trousseau's sign) or facial twitching (Chvostek's sign). This acute neuromuscular presentation, not a skeletal or soft-tissue change, is what follows within hours to days of parathyroid loss.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bone fractures from excess resorption are a feature of chronic PTH excess (hyperparathyroidism), not of acute PTH loss, which instead produces acute hypocalcemic tetany.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Overgrowth of soft tissues describes acromegaly (growth hormone excess), unrelated to parathyroid hormone loss.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Peripheral neuropathy is not the acute consequence of parathyroid loss; the acute picture is hypocalcemic tetany from increased neuromuscular excitability, not nerve damage.

questions.learning_objective: State that sudden loss of the parathyroid glands causes acute hypocalcemic tetany (skeletal muscle spasm).

questions.title: Acid-base consequence of aldosterone hypersecretion
questions.question: Which of the following is caused by hypersecretion of aldosterone?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Aldosterone increases renal sodium reabsorption, so it tends to raise, not lower, plasma sodium (or leave it near-normal via volume expansion) — hyponatremia is not the expected finding.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Aldosterone promotes potassium secretion at the collecting duct principal cells, producing hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia — the opposite direction from this option.
explanations.C: Correct. Aldosterone's sodium-potassium exchange at the collecting duct is coupled to hydrogen ion secretion into the tubular lumen. Sustained aldosterone excess therefore drives excess H+ loss in the urine alongside the K+ loss, producing a mild metabolic alkalosis. This alkalosis, paired with hypokalemia, is the classic biochemical signature of hyperaldosteronism.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Aldosterone-driven sodium and water retention expands extracellular volume and raises, not lowers, blood pressure — hyperaldosteronism classically causes hypertension, not hypotension.

questions.learning_objective: State that aldosterone hypersecretion causes a mild metabolic alkalosis, alongside hypokalemia and hypertension.

field_notes.conceptReuse: Reuses CON-END-01B09375D83562 (primary hyperaldosteronism concept minted for the Mock exam batch); that concept's own definition already documents the accompanying mild metabolic alkalosis, so this item's fact is a direct restatement rather than a new one.

questions.title: Effect of antidiuretic hormone on the distal nephron
questions.question: What is the effect of ADH?

options.A: Increase permeability of distal tubules to water

explanations.A: Correct. ADH (vasopressin) binds V2 receptors on principal cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct, inserting aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membrane. This increases the segment's water permeability, allowing water to be reabsorbed down the medullary osmotic gradient and the urine to be concentrated.
explanations.B: Incorrect. ADH's action is on water handling, not sodium transport; it does not increase sodium excretion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. By increasing water reabsorption, ADH decreases urine volume (antidiuresis) — the opposite of this option.
explanations.D: Incorrect. ADH promotes water retention, which expands plasma volume; it is not a hypotensive hormone (at very high, non-physiological concentrations vasopressin is even a vasoconstrictor).

questions.learning_objective: State that ADH increases the water permeability of the distal tubule/collecting duct.

field_notes.conceptReuse: Reuses CON-REN-106A6BC5BA462A (minted for the Mock exam's ADH-deficiency item, which names this same distal-tubule water-permeability mechanism from its absence); this item tests the same mechanism stated positively.

questions.title: Reabsorption in the diluting segment
questions.question: Which of the following are reabsorbed in the diluting segment?

explanations.A: Correct. The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle is called the 'diluting segment' precisely because it reabsorbs sodium and chloride via the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter while remaining essentially impermeable to water. Removing solute without water dilutes the tubular fluid, so what leaves this segment is hypotonic relative to plasma — the defining feature tested here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. If water were reabsorbed alongside sodium, the tubular fluid would not become dilute; the diluting segment's defining property is that it stays water-impermeable while removing solute.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ammonium handling is a proximal tubule and collecting duct acid-base function, not the diluting segment's defining transport.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Water is not reabsorbed here (the segment is water-impermeable), and urea reabsorption is instead a feature of the inner medullary collecting duct.

questions.learning_objective: State that the diluting segment (thick ascending limb) reabsorbs sodium and chloride without water.

questions.title: Factor that increases glomerular filtration rate
questions.question: Which of the following increases GFR?

explanations.A: Correct. GFR is the product of net filtration pressure and the filtration coefficient (Kf), which reflects glomerular capillary surface area and permeability. Raising Kf directly raises GFR for any given filtration pressure, making it a straightforward determinant among the four options.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Afferent arteriole constriction reduces glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure and blood flow into the glomerulus, which lowers, not raises, GFR.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Efferent arteriole dilation lowers resistance to outflow, reducing glomerular capillary pressure and GFR; it is efferent constriction (in moderation) that raises GFR.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sympathetic stimulation constricts the afferent arteriole (and reduces renal blood flow generally), lowering GFR rather than increasing it.

questions.learning_objective: Identify an increased filtration coefficient as a factor that raises GFR, distinguishing it from afferent constriction, efferent dilation and sympathetic stimulation, which all lower it.

questions.title: Minimal urine pH limiting hydrogen ion secretion
questions.question: What is the minimal PH of urine below which no H secretion occurs?

explanations.A: Incorrect. 7.4 is the normal plasma/arterial pH, far above the maximally acidified urine value; it is not a limiting value for tubular H+ secretion.
explanations.B: Correct. The renal tubular H+-secreting pumps can generate a maximum lumen-to-blood H+ gradient. This gradient allows urine to be acidified down to a floor of about pH 4.5. Below this value the gradient becomes too steep for the transporters to continue pumping H+ against it, so further net H+ secretion stops.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A urine pH of 6 is well above the kidney's true maximal acidifying capacity and does not represent the limiting value.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A urine pH of 5 is more acidic than typical resting urine but still not as low as the kidney's true minimum, which is closer to 4.5.

questions.learning_objective: State that the kidney can acidify urine to a minimum pH of about 4.5, below which tubular H+ secretion cannot continue.

questions.title: Maximum tubular secretion of PAH
questions.question: What is the maximum tubular secretion of para-amino hippuric acid in an adult?

explanations.A: Incorrect. 100 mg/min is above the figure printed in this source's own answer key for the maximal tubular secretory capacity (Tm) of PAH.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 150 mg/min substantially overstates the Tm for PAH secretion as keyed by this source.
explanations.C: Correct. As printed in this source's key, the maximal tubular secretory capacity (Tm) for para-amino hippuric acid in an adult is 75 mg/min — the plateau reached once the proximal tubule's organic-anion secretory carriers are saturated, beyond which further increases in plasma PAH do not increase its secretion rate. (Some texts quote a Tm closer to 80 mg/min; this source's key is kept per this lane's printed-key convention.)
explanations.D: Incorrect. 60 mg/min understates the figure printed in this source's answer key for PAH's tubular secretory maximum.

questions.learning_objective: State, per this source's own key, that the maximal tubular secretory capacity for PAH is 75 mg/min.

questions.title: Level of the micturition reflex
questions.question: Which of the following causes micturition reflex?

explanations.A: Correct. The micturition reflex is fundamentally a spinal reflex: bladder wall stretch receptors signal via the sacral spinal cord (S2-S4), which drives detrusor contraction and internal sphincter relaxation through the parasympathetic pelvic nerves. Higher centres (cortex, pontine micturition centre) modulate and can voluntarily inhibit or facilitate this reflex, but the basic reflex arc itself is spinal, which is why the reflex persists (as an uninhibited reflex bladder) after spinal cord injury above the sacral segments.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The cerebral cortex provides voluntary control and inhibition of micturition; it is not the site of the basic reflex arc, which is spinal.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The pontine micturition centre in the brain stem coordinates and facilitates the reflex, but it is not itself the reflex arc's level — the reflex is classified as spinal.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The sacral plexus is the nerve network through which the reflex's efferent and afferent fibres travel, but the reflex itself is described by its spinal cord level, not by the peripheral plexus name.

questions.learning_objective: State that the basic micturition reflex arc is a spinal reflex, modulated but not generated by higher centres.

questions.title: Manifestation of adrenal virilism
questions.question: Which of the following is a manifestation of adrenal virilism?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A moon face is a feature of glucocorticoid excess (Cushing syndrome), not specifically of androgen-driven adrenal virilism.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hyperpigmentation is a feature of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease), driven by excess ACTH/MSH-related peptides, not of androgen excess.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Tetany reflects hypocalcemia (as from parathyroid loss), unrelated to adrenal androgen excess.
explanations.D: Correct. Adrenal virilism results from excess adrenal androgen secretion (e.g. from an androgen-secreting adrenal tumour or congenital adrenal hyperplasia). Excess androgen drives hirsutism — excess terminal hair growth in a male-pattern distribution — along with other virilizing features such as acne, voice deepening and, in children, precocious pubic/facial hair. Hirsutism is the classic clinical manifestation tested for this androgen-excess state.

questions.learning_objective: Identify hirsutism as the classic manifestation of adrenal virilism (androgen excess).

questions.title: Testosterone's effect in fetal development
questions.question: Which of the following is an effect of testosterone in fetal development?

options.D: Development of penis, scrotum, and testis

explanations.A: Incorrect. Androgens promote body and facial hair growth but characteristically cause scalp hair thinning/loss (androgenic alopecia) later in life — the opposite of stimulating scalp hair — and this is not a fetal effect in any case.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bone growth is driven mainly by growth hormone/IGF-1 and, at puberty, sex steroids acting on the epiphyses; it is not testosterone's defining fetal action.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Enlargement of the penis is a pubertal, not fetal, androgen effect; in fetal life testosterone (via DHT) drives formation, not enlargement, of the external genitalia.
explanations.D: Correct. In fetal life, testosterone (converted locally to dihydrotestosterone by 5-alpha reductase) drives virilization of the external genitalia — differentiation and development of the penis and scrotum from the genital tubercle and labioscrotal folds — and supports testicular development and descent. This fetal androgen action is what determines male external genital phenotype, distinct from testosterone's separate pubertal actions of penile enlargement and bone/muscle growth.

questions.learning_objective: State that fetal testosterone (via DHT) drives development of the penis, scrotum and testis, distinguishing this from testosterone's later pubertal effects.
questions.module_subject: AU-MED-201 > Physiology > Testosterone and Fetal Sexual Differentiation

questions.title: Effect of parathyroid hormone
questions.question: Which of the following is an effect of PTH?

explanations.A: Correct. PTH's net skeletal effect, and the one tested by this source's key, is to increase bone resorption — mobilising calcium and phosphate from bone into plasma to raise plasma calcium. This resorptive action, together with increased renal calcium reabsorption and stimulation of renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase (raising active vitamin D and intestinal calcium absorption), is how PTH defends plasma calcium.
explanations.B: Incorrect. While PTH signals partly through osteoblastic receptors (which then signal osteoclasts), 'activation of osteoblast' alone does not capture PTH's net calcemic action, which is resorptive rather than bone-forming.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Bone mineralization is the opposite of PTH's net effect; PTH's role is to increase resorption and release calcium from bone, not to mineralize it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. PTH increases, not decreases, renal calcium reabsorption — it reduces urinary calcium excretion (while increasing phosphate excretion), the opposite of this option.

questions.learning_objective: State that PTH's net skeletal effect is to increase bone resorption, raising plasma calcium.
questions.module_subject: AU-MED-201 > Physiology > Parathyroid Hormone and Calcium Homeostasis

questions.title: Cause of anemia in renal insufficiency
questions.question: What's the cause of anemia in patients with renal insufficiency?

explanations.A: Correct. Erythropoietin is produced mainly by peritubular fibroblast-like cells of the renal cortex in response to hypoxia, and it drives red cell precursor proliferation and maturation in the bone marrow. As functioning renal mass is lost in chronic renal insufficiency, erythropoietin production falls, and this deficiency — not marrow failure or blood loss — is the principal cause of the normochromic, normocytic anemia of chronic kidney disease.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Renin secretion is not the driver of renal anemia; renin governs the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis for blood pressure/volume, unrelated to erythropoiesis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hemolysis is not the typical mechanism of renal anemia; the anemia of chronic kidney disease is primarily hypoproliferative, from reduced erythropoietin drive, not increased red cell destruction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cortisol is not characteristically increased in renal insufficiency, and it is not the mechanism of this anemia in any case.

questions.learning_objective: State that erythropoietin deficiency, from loss of functioning renal mass, is the cause of the anemia of chronic renal insufficiency.
questions.module_subject: AU-MED-201 > Physiology > Erythropoietin and Renal Anemia

questions.title: Nephron site of glucose reabsorption
questions.question: The filtered glucose is mostly reabsorbed from which part of the nephron?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The distal convoluted tubule is not the major site of glucose reabsorption; it is downstream of where essentially all filtered glucose has already been reclaimed under normal conditions.
explanations.B: Correct. The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs essentially all (about 100%, up to the transport maximum) of the filtered glucose load, via SGLT2 (early PCT, high-capacity/low-affinity) and SGLT1 (late PCT, low-capacity/high-affinity) sodium-glucose cotransporters on the apical membrane. This is why glucose is normally absent from urine, and why SGLT2 inhibitor drugs, which block this proximal reabsorption, are used to lower blood glucose in diabetes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The loop of Henle is not a significant site of glucose reabsorption; its transport is dominated by NaCl and water/urea handling for the countercurrent mechanism.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The cortical collecting duct handles late sodium, potassium and water/acid-base regulation, not bulk glucose reabsorption.

questions.learning_objective: State that the proximal convoluted tubule is the site of essentially all filtered glucose reabsorption.

questions.title: Trigger of ovulation
questions.question: Which of the following causes ovulation?

options.D: Second meiotic division of the oocyte

explanations.A: Incorrect. The corpus luteum forms from the ruptured follicle after ovulation has already occurred, so it is a consequence of ovulation, not its cause.
explanations.B: Correct. Rising estrogen from the dominant follicle triggers a surge of luteinizing hormone from the anterior pituitary; per this source's key, this LH surge occurs about 48 hours before ovulation and is the proximate hormonal trigger for follicular rupture and oocyte release. (Many texts describe the LH surge-to-ovulation interval as closer to 36 hours; this source's key is kept per this lane's printed-key convention.)
explanations.C: Incorrect. Progesterone secretion rises after ovulation, driven by the newly formed corpus luteum; it is a downstream consequence, not the trigger, of ovulation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The oocyte's resumption of meiosis (completing the first meiotic division and arresting again in metaphase II) is triggered by the LH surge and occurs around the time of ovulation, but it is a consequence of the same LH surge rather than the ovulation-causing event itself.

questions.learning_objective: State, per this source's own key, that a luteinizing hormone surge roughly 48 hours beforehand is the trigger for ovulation.
questions.module_subject: AU-MED-201 > Physiology > Ovulation and the Menstrual Cycle

questions.title: Role of the vasa recta in the countercurrent mechanism
questions.question: What is the role of vasa recta in counter current mechanism?

options.A: Maintaining the hyperosmolality of the interstitial fluid
options.B: Secrete sodium and chloride in renal tubules
options.C: Reabsorb sodium and water from renal tubules

explanations.A: Correct. The vasa recta are hairpin peritubular capillaries that run alongside the loop of Henle into the medulla. Through passive countercurrent exchange along their descending and ascending limbs, they remove reabsorbed water and solute from the medullary interstitium slowly and without net washout, which is what lets them maintain the steep corticomedullary osmotic gradient already established by the loop of Henle's countercurrent multiplier.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The vasa recta are blood vessels exchanging solute and water passively with the interstitium; they do not secrete sodium and chloride into the renal tubules, which is a tubular epithelial function, not a capillary one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Reabsorption of sodium and water from the tubular lumen back into blood is performed by the tubular epithelium and peritubular capillaries generally; describing the vasa recta's countercurrent role this way misses their gradient-preserving function specifically.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Creating the medullary hyperosmolar gradient is the loop of Henle's countercurrent multiplier's role; the vasa recta preserve, rather than create, a gradient already established by the loop.

questions.learning_objective: State that the vasa recta's function is to maintain, not create, the medullary interstitial osmotic gradient.
questions.module_subject: AU-MED-201 > Physiology > Renal Medullary Countercurrent Mechanism

questions.title: Adrenal cortex tumor with hypertension and diabetes
questions.question: A female patient was having DM, hypertension, and purple stria on skin. Upon examination, a tumor in adrenal cortex was found. What's your diagnosis?

explanations.A: Correct. A cortisol-secreting adrenal cortex tumour explains this picture: hyperglycemia from cortisol's gluconeogenic/anti-insulin effects, hypertension from cortisol's mineralocorticoid-like and vasopressor actions, and purple abdominal striae from cortisol-driven skin protein catabolism and thinning. This is primary Cushing syndrome — an ACTH-independent, adrenal source of excess cortisol. The tumour is found within the adrenal cortex itself here, not arising from a pituitary source.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Secondary Cushing (Cushing disease) is driven by excess ACTH from a pituitary corticotroph adenoma, which causes bilateral adrenal hyperplasia rather than a discrete adrenal tumour; this vignette instead locates the tumour in the adrenal cortex itself, making it primary (adrenal), not secondary.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Addison's disease is primary adrenal insufficiency (hypocortisolism), the opposite clinical and biochemical picture from this hypercortisolism vignette.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Conn's syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism) classically causes hypertension with hypokalemia, but not the hyperglycemia and purple striae driven specifically by glucocorticoid excess described here.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise hyperglycemia, hypertension and purple striae with an adrenal cortex tumour as primary (ACTH-independent) Cushing syndrome, distinguishing it from secondary Cushing, Addison's disease and Conn's syndrome.

questions.title: Pregnancy hormone measurable in urine
questions.question: Which pregnancy hormone could be measured in urine?

explanations.A: Correct. Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast from soon after implantation. It is excreted in sufficient concentration in urine to form the basis of standard urine pregnancy tests. These tests detect hCG, or its beta subunit, directly from a urine sample, which is why hCG is the pregnancy hormone tested for in a home or clinic urine test.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Human chorionic somatomammotropin (hCS, also called human placental lactogen) is a placental hormone, but it is assessed from maternal serum, not by a routine urine test, unlike hCG.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Luteinizing hormone is a pituitary gonadotropin used in ovulation-prediction urine tests, but it is not itself a pregnancy hormone or the marker used to detect pregnancy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Progesterone is measured from serum (or its urinary metabolite pregnanediol in specialised assays), not by the standard urine test used to detect or confirm pregnancy.

questions.learning_objective: State that hCG is the pregnancy hormone measured in standard urine pregnancy tests.
